text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to the Health Report with me, Norman
Swan. Today, so-called environmentally sound green textiles. Are some of them
actually woven over the damaged lives of the workers who produce them?
Protecting children's brains from the toxic effects of poverty. Important findings
for women with breast cancer that could save them from unnecessary treatment.
Important findings for people who have been treated for bowel cancer which
could save them a whole lot of anxiety and time.

When you buy a piece of clothing that has viscose or rayon in it, or when you see
some cellophane wrapping, you should spare a thought for the people who have
been involved in the manufacture of the raw material. According to a new book
there is a huge burden of serious brain and heart damage among workers in the
manufacturing process which has been known for over 100 years and persists to
this day, even in rich nations. The book is called Fake Silk: The Lethal History of
Viscose Rayon, and it's by Paul Blanc who is Professor of Medicine at the
University of California, San Francisco, and chief of UCSF's Division of
Occupational and Environmental Medicine.

Paul Blanc: Viscose has been used for a lot of things, not just textiles, but rayon
is viscose turned into thread and then turned into synthetic cellulose based
textile, it was really the very first synthetic textile. But the exact same chemistry
leads to cellophane, and what people probably don't realise is a lot of the
synthetic sponges that we use every day are mostly viscose as well. And then
there's some other specialty uses such as viscose film casings for sausage, what
we like to call in America 'skinless weenie'.

Norman Swan: Kind of a harmless phrase for something whose manufacture,
you say, is incredibly toxic. So essentially the chemistry goes back to the 18th
and 19th centuries.

Paul Blanc: That's right, the chemistry of viscose goes back to the very end of
the 19th century, turn of the 20th century. The main toxic chemical involved
which is called carbon disulphide was actually before that a very big chemical in
the rubber industry.
 
Norman Swan: And carbon disulphide, they first of all didn't know what to do
with it, but then it became very obvious that it was a really useful solvent to
dissolve other stuff.

Paul Blanc: Yes, it's an incredible solvent, it's very special. And that's why it has
really been only carbon disulphide that has worked in this viscose process. There
is an alternative chemical that has been developed in the last couple of decades
that is not very widely used, but basically the name of the game has been carbon
disulphide.

Norman Swan: So to make viscose, to make rayon, take us through the process,
what happens?

Paul Blanc: It's a pretty simple process. What you do is you take wood pulp or
some other source of cellulose, grind it up, bleach it, and then you add caustic to
it, let it sit around for a while, then you put into it carbon disulphide and it turns it
into this yellowy toxic syrup that you force through tubes into a bath of sulphuric
acid. And then the cellulose is regenerated as thread, or you can regenerate it as
a thin film, and that's the process. And what happens is it's pure cellulose again,
the carbon disulphide flies off. Unfortunately it flies off into the air that the
workers are breathing, unless you take special precautions which most of the
time they didn't.

Norman Swan: And of course this cellulose has been reinvented as a natural
fibre that is harmless, which in fact it is once it's reconstituted.

Paul Blanc: That's correct, and it is being marketed as a green product. I like to
call it green washing, because it's really quite cynical. They like to even push that
theme harder instead of wood pulp from trees they use bamboo, it's the
posterchild for renewable.

Norman Swan: So when you wear clothes that have been reconstituted from
bamboo, this is the process we are talking about, by and large.

Paul Blanc: Absolutely.

Norman Swan: Even now in the 21st century.

Paul Blanc: Oh yes.
 
Norman Swan: So take us through the history then of how it has affected
workers.

Paul Blanc: The very first toxic effect was that it drove workers insane. They
would develop acute psychosis. There was a famous rubber factory in the 19th
century that had iron bars on its second-storey window because the workers
were so prone to jump out and kill themselves.

Norman Swan: You're kidding!

Paul Blanc: No, I'm not making this up. And through the 20th century there were
multiple reports of insanity, people killing themselves, people killing other people,
mostly in the viscose rayon industry but there were other sources of exposure
too. It was used in the United States, I don't know about Australia, but the United
States it was the preferred gopher poison. You would put it down gopher holes
because it's heavier than air, and kill gophers. And there was a report of these
two brothers who had a 20-gallon can of this stuff and it was leaking
unbeknownst to them, and one of them went completely crazy and murdered
somebody and then kill themselves. These stories just are kind of out there in the
literature.

Norman Swan: Did the employers of these people recognise that this was an
industrial problem? What was the response to this clear association between the
manufacturing process and people developing psychosis?

Paul Blanc: Well, there was a kind of split. When rayon came to be marketed
they basically tried to forget all the things that had been learned from the same
chemical and the rubber industry. I can't prove that they suppressed knowledge,
but there certainly was no impetus to publish very much of anything. The big
centres, the biggest of them being Great Britain at the time, didn't publish any
information at all, and it went for another two decades before it started being
published. When the first big study was done systematically in the United States
in the 1930s, the late 1930s, they found that about 30% of the working population
exposed demonstrated pretty severe effects.

Norman Swan: And it wasn't just neurological, it was cardiovascular as well, it
affected the heart.
 
Paul Blanc: Well, that was only able to be shown much later because the
techniques to show an increased death rate from heart attack and stroke are
much more sophisticated. It was really the 1960s. That is an example where
there was a smoking gun where you can show that Courtaulds did everything
that could to keep those data from being published in Great Britain.

Norman Swan: So were there no whistleblowers at that time, no doctors who
were saying 'I'm seeing this, why aren't you doing something about it', there was
no noise?

Paul Blanc: There were doctors and other people agitating, but in fact it's not so
easy to get the word out, but articles would appear in big journals and in
newspapers, and then everything would be forgotten again.

Norman Swan: So there was no response in terms of industrial hygiene, better
ventilation, isolating the mix so that the vapour doesn't come off or trying to
prevent the vapour coming off?

Paul Blanc: There were some efforts, but in fact there was always resistance or
reluctance to accept that the levels which were purported to be safe were not
safe, so even when there were reduced levels, that was still way too high. That
still reflected in the standard in the United States where the legal limit is 20 parts
per million. So the standard in the United States is still legally 20 parts per
million, even though the United States research agency has recommended that
the level be significantly lower than that, one part per million, 20 times more
protective.

Norman Swan: World War II is where rayon really took off.

Paul Blanc: Well, it took off before that in fact because in the Depression,
despite worldwide economic collapse, the rayon industry was really growing
logarithmically, and that's just continued through the war where it was a strategic
material. But even before that it was very big business, not just in Britain and the
United States, Germany, Italy, Japan were all huge producers. Official German
policy actually was to mix rayon into other fabrics, and that's what we have today.
When you buy something that will say 20% viscose, that's the typical kinds of
viscose blends that we have nowadays, and that actually lead to higher exposure
in the workers because the technology was they would pull this long a bunch of
 
threads called a tow, dripping with carbon disulphide, out of the vat, and people
got even more exposure that way. And then in the war, in occupied Europe, the
Germans really manufactured their rayon with slave labour across the continent.

Norman Swan: And you found one factory that was only eight kilometres from
Theresienstadt, the concentration camp.

Paul Blanc: That's correct, but there were other factories, and we have records
because one of the important French resistance fighters, a woman who was
arrested very early in the occupation, was sent as a slave labourer to one of the
other German factories and after the war wrote a memoir of her experiences. Of
course she didn't know what she was working with, only that it made her blind
and burned her fingers.

Norman Swan: We are still producing rayon today but in developing countries.

Paul Blanc: Rayon as fibre is in China and Indonesia and India. We know almost
nothing about the conditions, particularly in Indonesia and India, although we
have a sense from limited reports that it's not very good. But it's important to
remember that other viscose products are produced still in Europe and North
America and elsewhere, but the textile business has largely gone to those
countries, and Thailand I think is a producer as well.

Norman Swan: Is your suspicion then that when you wear something that's got
viscose in it, it could be built on the pyre of a 30% rate of disability from toxicity
due to carbon disulphide?

Paul Blanc: It may not be that high anymore, although who knows what it is in
these factories in India. I would say largely yes when you buy that shirt for $12 in
the warehouse store that should really cost three times that amount but the
reason you got it so cheaply is that some unfortunate in a 15th-floor death trap
lock-up in Bangladesh made it for 10c a day. It is no risk to you from wearing that
shirt, the same thing with anything made of rayon.

Norman Swan: You obviously wrote this book with a sense of outrage. Has there
been litigation? Has DuPont, Courtaulds or whatever Courtaulds has become
since then, have they suffered litigation as a result of this?
 
Paul Blanc: In the United States you can't sue your employer. The workers
compensation system in the United States precludes suing your employer. In
Great Britain they have a system where a disease has to be officially recognised
in order to be easily compensatable. And although certain effects from carbon
disulphide are recognised in Great Britain, they never did recognise heart attack
as being potentially related, despite the epidemiologic evidence that was quite
convincing.

Norman Swan: So what's the lesson?

Paul Blanc: Well, one lesson is that knowledge is power, and that when a brand-
new product comes on the market like rayon with such a highfalutin new product
at the time, we should think about what is behind that technology, what are the
risks and what are the benefits and who is getting the benefit and who suffers the
risk.

Norman Swan: And in terms of industrial safety?

Paul Blanc: In terms of industrial safety I think it's an ongoing struggle that has
not particularly progressed in the last 100 years the way one might have hoped.

Norman Swan: Just broadening it out and finally my question is related to
problems that affect just workers in an industry or problems that escaped to the
general community, and it strikes me that asbestos, because it escaped to the
general community, got a lot of attention. Do we still have an issue where it's just
the worker who gets affected rather than the general community where it tends to
be buried still, versus toxins which escape, if you like, into the general
environment and affect the general community, that we have a double standard.

Paul Blanc: I think you are absolutely correct, that is very much the case.

Norman Swan: Paul Blanc is Professor of Medicine at the University of
California, San Francisco, and chief of UCSF's Division of Occupational and
Environmental Medicine. The book is called Fake Silk: The Lethal History of
Viscose Rayon, and the publisher is Yale University Press.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC
Radio across Canada.
 
Two reviews of the latest evidence on early breast cancer and people who have
been treated for bowel cancer which hasn't yet spread have good news. A lot of
time, inconvenience, expense and anxiety could be saved. And author on both of
these reviews was Brigid Hickey, a radiation oncologist at Princess Alexandra
Hospital in Brisbane. Let's start with women who just have the lump removed and
need radiation therapy afterwards. The debate is over how many fractions they
need, how many sessions of radiotherapy.

Brigid Hickey: What we did was searched extensively the literature, published
and unpublished, around the world according to the principles of the Cochrane
collaboration methodology.

Norman Swan: So to explain here, we are talking about a systematic review
where you take all the evidence and you stir it up, remix it, reanalyse it to see
where the balance lies of evidence.

Brigid Hickey: That's right. And the question was is using fewer treatments as
good as using the standard 25 to 30 treatments, as good in terms of breast
cancer outcomes, survival, and the cosmetic outcome, because remember that
breast conservation is all about the cosmetic outcome.

Norman Swan: And just forgive me if I'm missing something here, I'd have
thought that fewer fractions would have no impact on the cosmetic result. Why
would you expect less radiotherapy to make the breast look any different?

Brigid Hickey: That's to do with the dose per fraction. If you are
hypofractionating, where you give a bigger dose per fraction, that can be
associated with more late effects on slow reacting tissues that cause more
fibrosis and more scarring.

Norman Swan: So essentially what we are talking about here is that you get a
certain dose, if you like, in total of your radiation therapy over a period of five or
six weeks, and the idea is you get the same dose but in a much shorter period of
time.

Brigid Hickey: Roughly the same dose, yes.

Norman Swan: Which means that each zap is going to be stronger.
 
Brigid Hickey: That's right.

Norman Swan: Okay, so you looked at all the available evidence from
randomised trials. What did you find?

Brigid Hickey: Well, we looked at over 8,000 women in nine studies, and we
found that there is no difference in local control or cosmetic outcome, overall
survival, or breast cancer specific or relapse-free survival. So the outcomes that
matter to the doctors who want to control the cancer and the patients, there is no
difference, so it is safe.

Norman Swan: And the woman has been less inconvenienced because she
hasn't had to turn up in a radiation therapy department so often.

Brigid Hickey: Absolutely.

Norman Swan: And how many days does this save?

Brigid Hickey: Conventional treatment would be 25 to 30 treatments, five
treatments a week.

Norman Swan: So that's five or six weeks. And hypofractionated?

Brigid Hickey: Would be 15 to 16 treatments, so just over three weeks. You can
imagine for busy women who are working with children, it's a great saving in
terms of their time. We know that if you live a long way from a radiation therapy
department you may be more likely to choose mastectomy based on the fact that
you don't want to be away from your family and your work for six weeks, and then
it saves money, time, resources, and can mean that we can treat more patients.

Norman Swan: So some women choose mastectomy because they can't deal
with the inconvenience of the radiotherapy?

Brigid Hickey: Yes, that's right.

Norman Swan: Before you have all your colleagues not talking to you any more,
we pay…apart from the public sector, in the private sector they get paid per
fraction, so they are going to get paid less if they don't do hypofractionated. So
 
there must be quite significant disincentives to actually do this because people
are going to lose money.

Brigid Hickey: Changing practice is difficult. There has been more adoption of
hypofractionation, and in fact it's one of the big moves in radiation oncology at
the moment, is the move towards hypofractionation, not only in breast cancer,
also in prostate cancer. And I think now we can say with the results of this review
that really it's just as good and just as safe.

People had a theoretical concern that using larger doses per fraction when the
heart vessels were irradiated might be associated with increased cardiovascular
morbidity and mortality, but these days we've got more techniques that we can
use to actually avoid irradiating the heart, so that takes out that argument.

Norman Swan: And so is there evidence that in the private sector you're more
likely to get the longer course than the short course?

Brigid Hickey: I'm not aware of evidence…

Norman Swan: But really the message here for women when they are being
referred for radiation oncology, whether it's the public or private sector is ask for
hypofractionated and the shortest course that has got the evidence behind it.

Brigid Hickey: At least discuss it. For some women with large breasts we are
concerned about using hypo fractionated technique because there might be more
late toxicity, but we can, again, deal with that by other techniques such as
treating women lying on their stomach and that reduces the dimension of the
breast and makes it more possible to use hypofractionation.

Norman Swan: A second Cochrane review you've just been involved with
involves follow-up of people who have been treated for colorectal cancer, in other
words, bowel cancer, which hasn't spread. So it's a common cancer, one of the
commonest, and of course a lot of our outpatient resources are taken up with
people with follow-up, and that means that new people with a new problem that
needs to be diagnosed don't get in to see doctors because they are cramped with
follow-up. And so you've been looking at really what sort of follow-up people
need after a potentially curative surgery for bowel cancer.
 
Brigid Hickey: Absolutely. The genesis of this review was when I was working in
New Zealand. And as you know, New Zealand and Australia have got the highest
incidence of colorectal cancer in the world, and we were understaffed and we
were seeing so many people, and we wondered whether we were actually
benefiting them. And when we recognised there was some controversy about
that we did this review. We didn't so much examine what the perfect follow-up
regime involves. What we looked at was does intensive follow-up, is it better than
less intense follow-up in terms of survival.

Norman Swan: And so what is intensive?

Brigid Hickey: In the studies involved it varied from some verses none, to very
intensive follow-up with lots of scans and MRIs and CTs.

Norman Swan: And so what did you find?

Brigid Hickey: Well, we were quite shocked because the latest iteration of this
review, we don't find that there is any improvement in survival. In fact there is no
difference in overall survival between the two study arms, colorectal cancer,
specific survival is the same, and so is relapse-free survival.

You do more salvage operations and you find fewer recurrences outside the
setting of the clinic visit, but the survival is the same. So that has put what we
know turned on its head, which is a little bit confronting. I suppose both reviews
have got the theme that more is not always better.

Norman Swan: So somebody who is listening to this who has had a bowel
cancer removed and it hasn't spread, have you landed on what is the sweet point
for follow-up?

Brigid Hickey: I have to say we haven't. That really was not something we were
able to tease out of the data.

Norman Swan: So just give me the middle ground then in this study. I know it
was very different and so on, but was it every three months you get a
colonoscopy or once a year you come back and we do an MRI scan or we just do
a rectal examination and feel your tummy? What was kind of the middle ground?
 
Brigid Hickey: Kind of the middle ground was probably a CT once a year,
colonoscopy once a year, CT looking at lungs and liver, and blood tests looking
at a marker called CEA. We weren't able to demonstrate that the use of tumour
markers improved survival. And this study spanned a long time interval, so over
that time things have changed, investigations have become more sophisticated
and the surgery has become more sophisticated. So we wondered whether we
had got better at doing the operations to remove, for example, a solitary liver
metastasis, and the post-operative care had got better, but we weren't able to
demonstrate any difference looking by study age. So it was a very robust result.

We've always known there is a population of patients who have a solitary liver
metastasis, for example, diagnosed, if they have it excised they have a long
survival, and that has been reported and known for a long time. But without doing
a randomised control trial, you don't know whether those patients just had
indolent disease and they would have been okay without it being removed.

The other thing that might be happening now is that we have more effective
systemic treatments when you do have metastatic disease, and that might be
narrowing the gap so that if you do have metastatic disease diagnosed you have
better survival because there's more effective chemotherapy.

Norman Swan: So in other words, the implication of that is that if you have a less
intensive regime and the tumour does come back in between times, the
treatment is better?

Brigid Hickey: That's possible.

Norman Swan: Or it makes no difference at all and you might as well just wait
the year and get the CT scan.

Brigid Hickey: Yes.

Norman Swan: But obviously what needs to happen now is studies need to be
done to work out what is the optimal regime. It's a mess.

Brigid Hickey: Yes.
 
Norman Swan: So Brigid, knowing what you know now, if you were unfortunate
enough to develop an uncomplicated bowel cancer, you had curative surgery,
what would you want to have done to you as follow-up?

Brigid Hickey: Great question. I'd probably still have a CT scan once a year.

Norman Swan: Just to keep yourself comfortable.

Brigid Hickey: Well, it would probably make me very anxious.

Norman Swan: And that's the other problem, is the more you do, the more
anxiety there is.

Brigid Hickey: There's a word for it, scan anxiety, scanxiety. One of the things
we wanted to look at in this was the harms of follow-up, because every day I see
patients who come and see me wound-up, anxious because they are coming to
see me and am I going to find a recurrence. And we've got to know that we are
benefiting people in order to put them through that.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much indeed.

Brigid Hickey: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Brigid Hickey is a radiation oncologist at Princess Alexandra
Hospital in Brisbane.

There are many factors that affect children's development, from the genes they
inherit from their parents, the age of their father at conception, and their
environment, especially if there is poverty. Poverty is well known to be toxic to
children. A study in the southern United States where they have the worst
poverty in the nation has looked at the brain scans of young people who have
spent years growing up in deprivation to see if a parenting program made any
difference. One of the researchers was Gene Brody from the Centre for Family
Research at the University of Georgia, Athens.

Gene Brody: Economic hardship really rips the psychological fabric of the
parents rearing children. These parents work very hard, despite living in tough
circumstances, to do their best. But the chronic day-to-day stressors associated
with poverty made them feel badly, and for some children this had the
 
consequence of them not doing as well as they could or reaching their potential
in school and other areas. And this jived with other research from around the
world actually, that shows that children growing up in poverty conditions where
resources are scarce but stressors are plenty tend not to develop as well
academically and socially as children who aren't battling these particular kinds of
stressors.

Norman Swan: And you have some evidence that the brains were in fact
different.

Gene Brody: You know, there were clues there where researchers would
associate living in poverty with diminished brain development, and it made us
wonder, since we follow children from preadolescents through young adulthood,
whether children who spent more years living in poverty would have smaller brain
volumes in areas of the brain that were important for their academic
development, for their memory and for their ability to cope with stress. And
unfortunately we found it was, for some children.

Norman Swan: And which parts of the brain and what sort of functionality?

Gene Brody: The parts of the brain that we focused on where the hippocampus
and the amygdala.

Norman Swan: So that's memory, emotional control, that sort of thing.

Gene Brody: Right, yes.

Norman Swan: You also looked at an intervention called Strong African
American Families which was, what, a parenting program?

Gene Brody: Yes, in 2001, 2002 we developed a program for African American
families living in the rural south that was designed to mitigate stress by
enhancing the quality of care giving that children received. And we have studied
the effectiveness of this program to promote psychological adjustment, academic
achievement, and some health outcomes as well. And that caused us to wonder
if the benefits of this program would extend to brain development. Would youth,
who at age 11 lived more years in poverty and whose brain development was
assessed at age 25, not show the deleterious effects of poverty if they had
 
participated and received enhanced levels of parenting that were taught by the
Strong African American Families program?

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Gene Brody: We were delighted to find it did. So the association or the link
between poverty and diminished brain development was found only for children
who did not participate in the prevention program.

Norman Swan: And what were the elements of this program, what were you
teaching parents to do? Because you probably know in Australia we have
developed one particular parenting program which is quite popular
internationally. What were you doing with these parents, what were you teaching
them?

Gene Brody: First I want to give a shout-out to Professor Matt Sanders…

Norman Swan: At Griffith University.

Gene Brody: Whose prevention programs are internationally known. Our
program was a little different than Professor Sanders' in that the rural Southern
context that our participants grew up in are unique, and the parenting practices
that are successful in the 'black belt' might be different than parenting practices in
the northern parts of the United States or in very urban areas. So we spent 10
years documenting what were the parenting processes that enhanced the
development of children in the rural south. And we settled on and focused on a
few things that really tended to matter. And these things were providing
emotional support for children, increase the amount of time that parents spend
with their children, increase the use of a parenting dynamic which involves high
levels of control laced with high levels of warmth. The kids know that the reason
their parents are keeping them in tow and being very vigilant about their children
is that they often live in some dangerous circumstances which require that
protection. Another thing we did was to enhance how routinised the home
environments were.

Norman Swan: So making them less chaotic.
 
Gene Brody: Making them much less chaotic, much more predictable, making
sure there was a time and place for them to do their studies, and all the while
increasing their presence at their children's school. One of the things that we find
is the more that home environments are routinised and predictable and parents
show up at school, schools treat the parents differently and in turn the children
benefit more from the teacher's attention at school. And over time this particular
formulation of parenting practices really has been shown to aid not only
psychosocial development but health, and now it appears to expand into the
brain.

Norman Swan: And just finally, Gene Brody, the applicability to other areas?

Gene Brody: This program has now been disseminated into 40 communities
across the United States, and we are optimistic about its ability to continue to
enhance the development of African American youth, and time will tell.

Norman Swan: Thanks for joining us on the Health Report.

Gene Brody: Glad to be here, thank you for asking me.

Norman Swan: Gene Brody is the director of the Centre for Family Research at
the University of Georgia, Athens.

You've been listening to the Health Report, I'm Norman Swan, I hope you'll join
me next week.

call it green washing, because it's really quite cynical. They like to even push that
theme harder instead of wood pulp from trees they use bamboo, it's the
posterchild for renewable.

Norman Swan: So when you wear clothes that have been reconstituted from
bamboo, this is the process we are talking about, by and large.

Paul Blanc: Absolutely.

Norman Swan: Even now in the 21st century.

Paul Blanc: Oh yes.

Norman Swan: So take us through the history then of how it has affected
workers.

Paul Blanc: The very first toxic effect was that it drove workers insane. They
would develop acute psychosis. There was a famous rubber factory in the 19th
century that had iron bars on its second-storey window because the workers
were so prone to jump out and kill themselves.

Norman Swan: You're kidding!

Paul Blanc: No, I'm not making this up. And through the 20th century there were
multiple reports of insanity, people killing themselves, people killing other people,
mostly in the viscose rayon industry but there were other sources of exposure
too. It was used in the United States, I don't know about Australia, but the United
States it was the preferred gopher poison. You would put it down gopher holes
because it's heavier than air, and kill gophers. And there was a report of these
two brothers who had a 20-gallon can of this stuff and it was leaking
unbeknownst to them, and one of them went completely crazy and murdered
somebody and then kill themselves. These stories just are kind of out there in the
literature.

Norman Swan: Did the employers of these people recognise that this was an
industrial problem? What was the response to this clear association between the
manufacturing process and people developing psychosis?

Paul Blanc: Well, there was a kind of split. When rayon came to be marketed
they basically tried to forget all the things that had been learned from the same
chemical and the rubber industry. I can't prove that they suppressed knowledge,
but there certainly was no impetus to publish very much of anything. The big
centres, the biggest of them being Great Britain at the time, didn't publish any
information at all, and it went for another two decades before it started being
published. When the first big study was done systematically in the United States
in the 1930s, the late 1930s, they found that about 30% of the working population
exposed demonstrated pretty severe effects.

Norman Swan: And it wasn't just neurological, it was cardiovascular as well, it
affected the heart.

Paul Blanc: Well, that was only able to be shown much later because the
techniques to show an increased death rate from heart attack and stroke are
much more sophisticated. It was really the 1960s. That is an example where
there was a smoking gun where you can show that Courtaulds did everything
that could to keep those data from being published in Great Britain.

Norman Swan: So were there no whistleblowers at that time, no doctors who
were saying 'I'm seeing this, why aren't you doing something about it', there was
no noise?

Paul Blanc: There were doctors and other people agitating, but in fact it's not so
easy to get the word out, but articles would appear in big journals and in
newspapers, and then everything would be forgotten again.

Norman Swan: So there was no response in terms of industrial hygiene, better
ventilation, isolating the mix so that the vapour doesn't come off or trying to
prevent the vapour coming off?

Paul Blanc: There were some efforts, but in fact there was always resistance or
reluctance to accept that the levels which were purported to be safe were not
safe, so even when there were reduced levels, that was still way too high. That
still reflected in the standard in the United States where the legal limit is 20 parts
per million. So the standard in the United States is still legally 20 parts per
million, even though the United States research agency has recommended that
the level be significantly lower than that, one part per million, 20 times more
protective.

Norman Swan: World War II is where rayon really took off.

Paul Blanc: Well, it took off before that in fact because in the Depression,
despite worldwide economic collapse, the rayon industry was really growing
logarithmically, and that's just continued through the war where it was a strategic
material. But even before that it was very big business, not just in Britain and the
United States, Germany, Italy, Japan were all huge producers. Official German
policy actually was to mix rayon into other fabrics, and that's what we have today.
When you buy something that will say 20% viscose, that's the typical kinds of
viscose blends that we have nowadays, and that actually lead to higher exposure
in the workers because the technology was they would pull this long a bunch of

threads called a tow, dripping with carbon disulphide, out of the vat, and people
got even more exposure that way. And then in the war, in occupied Europe, the
Germans really manufactured their rayon with slave labour across the continent.

Norman Swan: And you found one factory that was only eight kilometres from
Theresienstadt, the concentration camp.

Paul Blanc: That's correct, but there were other factories, and we have records
because one of the important French resistance fighters, a woman who was
arrested very early in the occupation, was sent as a slave labourer to one of the
other German factories and after the war wrote a memoir of her experiences. Of
course she didn't know what she was working with, only that it made her blind
and burned her fingers.

Norman Swan: We are still producing rayon today but in developing countries.

Paul Blanc: Rayon as fibre is in China and Indonesia and India. We know almost
nothing about the conditions, particularly in Indonesia and India, although we
have a sense from limited reports that it's not very good. But it's important to
remember that other viscose products are produced still in Europe and North
America and elsewhere, but the textile business has largely gone to those
countries, and Thailand I think is a producer as well.

Norman Swan: Is your suspicion then that when you wear something that's got
viscose in it, it could be built on the pyre of a 30% rate of disability from toxicity
due to carbon disulphide?

Paul Blanc: It may not be that high anymore, although who knows what it is in
these factories in India. I would say largely yes when you buy that shirt for $12 in
the warehouse store that should really cost three times that amount but the
reason you got it so cheaply is that some unfortunate in a 15th-floor death trap
lock-up in Bangladesh made it for 10c a day. It is no risk to you from wearing that
shirt, the same thing with anything made of rayon.

Norman Swan: You obviously wrote this book with a sense of outrage. Has there
been litigation? Has DuPont, Courtaulds or whatever Courtaulds has become
since then, have they suffered litigation as a result of this?

Paul Blanc: In the United States you can't sue your employer. The workers
compensation system in the United States precludes suing your employer. In
Great Britain they have a system where a disease has to be officially recognised
in order to be easily compensatable. And although certain effects from carbon
disulphide are recognised in Great Britain, they never did recognise heart attack
as being potentially related, despite the epidemiologic evidence that was quite
convincing.

Norman Swan: So what's the lesson?

Paul Blanc: Well, one lesson is that knowledge is power, and that when a brand-
new product comes on the market like rayon with such a highfalutin new product
at the time, we should think about what is behind that technology, what are the
risks and what are the benefits and who is getting the benefit and who suffers the
risk.

Norman Swan: And in terms of industrial safety?

Paul Blanc: In terms of industrial safety I think it's an ongoing struggle that has
not particularly progressed in the last 100 years the way one might have hoped.

Norman Swan: Just broadening it out and finally my question is related to
problems that affect just workers in an industry or problems that escaped to the
general community, and it strikes me that asbestos, because it escaped to the
general community, got a lot of attention. Do we still have an issue where it's just
the worker who gets affected rather than the general community where it tends to
be buried still, versus toxins which escape, if you like, into the general
environment and affect the general community, that we have a double standard.

Paul Blanc: I think you are absolutely correct, that is very much the case.

Norman Swan: Paul Blanc is Professor of Medicine at the University of
California, San Francisco, and chief of UCSF's Division of Occupational and
Environmental Medicine. The book is called Fake Silk: The Lethal History of
Viscose Rayon, and the publisher is Yale University Press.

Two reviews of the latest evidence on early breast cancer and people who have
been treated for bowel cancer which hasn't yet spread have good news. A lot of
time, inconvenience, expense and anxiety could be saved. And author on both of
these reviews was Brigid Hickey, a radiation oncologist at Princess Alexandra
Hospital in Brisbane. Let's start with women who just have the lump removed and
need radiation therapy afterwards. The debate is over how many fractions they
need, how many sessions of radiotherapy.

Brigid Hickey: What we did was searched extensively the literature, published
and unpublished, around the world according to the principles of the Cochrane
collaboration methodology.

Norman Swan: So to explain here, we are talking about a systematic review
where you take all the evidence and you stir it up, remix it, reanalyse it to see
where the balance lies of evidence.

Brigid Hickey: That's right. And the question was is using fewer treatments as
good as using the standard 25 to 30 treatments, as good in terms of breast
cancer outcomes, survival, and the cosmetic outcome, because remember that
breast conservation is all about the cosmetic outcome.

Norman Swan: And just forgive me if I'm missing something here, I'd have
thought that fewer fractions would have no impact on the cosmetic result. Why
would you expect less radiotherapy to make the breast look any different?

Brigid Hickey: That's to do with the dose per fraction. If you are
hypofractionating, where you give a bigger dose per fraction, that can be
associated with more late effects on slow reacting tissues that cause more
fibrosis and more scarring.

Norman Swan: So essentially what we are talking about here is that you get a
certain dose, if you like, in total of your radiation therapy over a period of five or
six weeks, and the idea is you get the same dose but in a much shorter period of
time.

Brigid Hickey: Roughly the same dose, yes.

Norman Swan: Which means that each zap is going to be stronger.

Brigid Hickey: That's right.

Norman Swan: Okay, so you looked at all the available evidence from
randomised trials. What did you find?

Brigid Hickey: Well, we looked at over 8,000 women in nine studies, and we
found that there is no difference in local control or cosmetic outcome, overall
survival, or breast cancer specific or relapse-free survival. So the outcomes that
matter to the doctors who want to control the cancer and the patients, there is no
difference, so it is safe.

Norman Swan: And the woman has been less inconvenienced because she
hasn't had to turn up in a radiation therapy department so often.

Brigid Hickey: Absolutely.

Norman Swan: And how many days does this save?

Brigid Hickey: Conventional treatment would be 25 to 30 treatments, five
treatments a week.

Norman Swan: So that's five or six weeks. And hypofractionated?

Brigid Hickey: Would be 15 to 16 treatments, so just over three weeks. You can
imagine for busy women who are working with children, it's a great saving in
terms of their time. We know that if you live a long way from a radiation therapy
department you may be more likely to choose mastectomy based on the fact that
you don't want to be away from your family and your work for six weeks, and then
it saves money, time, resources, and can mean that we can treat more patients.

Norman Swan: So some women choose mastectomy because they can't deal
with the inconvenience of the radiotherapy?

Brigid Hickey: Yes, that's right.

Norman Swan: Before you have all your colleagues not talking to you any more,
we pay…apart from the public sector, in the private sector they get paid per
fraction, so they are going to get paid less if they don't do hypofractionated. So

there must be quite significant disincentives to actually do this because people
are going to lose money.

Brigid Hickey: Changing practice is difficult. There has been more adoption of
hypofractionation, and in fact it's one of the big moves in radiation oncology at
the moment, is the move towards hypofractionation, not only in breast cancer,
also in prostate cancer. And I think now we can say with the results of this review
that really it's just as good and just as safe.

People had a theoretical concern that using larger doses per fraction when the
heart vessels were irradiated might be associated with increased cardiovascular
morbidity and mortality, but these days we've got more techniques that we can
use to actually avoid irradiating the heart, so that takes out that argument.

Norman Swan: And so is there evidence that in the private sector you're more
likely to get the longer course than the short course?

Brigid Hickey: I'm not aware of evidence…

Norman Swan: But really the message here for women when they are being
referred for radiation oncology, whether it's the public or private sector is ask for
hypofractionated and the shortest course that has got the evidence behind it.

Brigid Hickey: At least discuss it. For some women with large breasts we are
concerned about using hypo fractionated technique because there might be more
late toxicity, but we can, again, deal with that by other techniques such as
treating women lying on their stomach and that reduces the dimension of the
breast and makes it more possible to use hypofractionation.

Norman Swan: A second Cochrane review you've just been involved with
involves follow-up of people who have been treated for colorectal cancer, in other
words, bowel cancer, which hasn't spread. So it's a common cancer, one of the
commonest, and of course a lot of our outpatient resources are taken up with
people with follow-up, and that means that new people with a new problem that
needs to be diagnosed don't get in to see doctors because they are cramped with
follow-up. And so you've been looking at really what sort of follow-up people
need after a potentially curative surgery for bowel cancer.

Brigid Hickey: Absolutely. The genesis of this review was when I was working in
New Zealand. And as you know, New Zealand and Australia have got the highest
incidence of colorectal cancer in the world, and we were understaffed and we
were seeing so many people, and we wondered whether we were actually
benefiting them. And when we recognised there was some controversy about
that we did this review. We didn't so much examine what the perfect follow-up
regime involves. What we looked at was does intensive follow-up, is it better than
less intense follow-up in terms of survival.

Norman Swan: And so what is intensive?

Brigid Hickey: In the studies involved it varied from some verses none, to very
intensive follow-up with lots of scans and MRIs and CTs.

Norman Swan: And so what did you find?

Brigid Hickey: Well, we were quite shocked because the latest iteration of this
review, we don't find that there is any improvement in survival. In fact there is no
difference in overall survival between the two study arms, colorectal cancer,
specific survival is the same, and so is relapse-free survival.

You do more salvage operations and you find fewer recurrences outside the
setting of the clinic visit, but the survival is the same. So that has put what we
know turned on its head, which is a little bit confronting. I suppose both reviews
have got the theme that more is not always better.

Norman Swan: So somebody who is listening to this who has had a bowel
cancer removed and it hasn't spread, have you landed on what is the sweet point
for follow-up?

Brigid Hickey: I have to say we haven't. That really was not something we were
able to tease out of the data.

Norman Swan: So just give me the middle ground then in this study. I know it
was very different and so on, but was it every three months you get a
colonoscopy or once a year you come back and we do an MRI scan or we just do
a rectal examination and feel your tummy? What was kind of the middle ground?

Brigid Hickey: Kind of the middle ground was probably a CT once a year,
colonoscopy once a year, CT looking at lungs and liver, and blood tests looking
at a marker called CEA. We weren't able to demonstrate that the use of tumour
markers improved survival. And this study spanned a long time interval, so over
that time things have changed, investigations have become more sophisticated
and the surgery has become more sophisticated. So we wondered whether we
had got better at doing the operations to remove, for example, a solitary liver
metastasis, and the post-operative care had got better, but we weren't able to
demonstrate any difference looking by study age. So it was a very robust result.

We've always known there is a population of patients who have a solitary liver
metastasis, for example, diagnosed, if they have it excised they have a long
survival, and that has been reported and known for a long time. But without doing
a randomised control trial, you don't know whether those patients just had
indolent disease and they would have been okay without it being removed.

The other thing that might be happening now is that we have more effective
systemic treatments when you do have metastatic disease, and that might be
narrowing the gap so that if you do have metastatic disease diagnosed you have
better survival because there's more effective chemotherapy.

Norman Swan: So in other words, the implication of that is that if you have a less
intensive regime and the tumour does come back in between times, the
treatment is better?

Brigid Hickey: That's possible.

Norman Swan: Or it makes no difference at all and you might as well just wait
the year and get the CT scan.

Brigid Hickey: Yes.

Norman Swan: But obviously what needs to happen now is studies need to be
done to work out what is the optimal regime. It's a mess.

Brigid Hickey: Yes.

Norman Swan: So Brigid, knowing what you know now, if you were unfortunate
enough to develop an uncomplicated bowel cancer, you had curative surgery,
what would you want to have done to you as follow-up?

Brigid Hickey: Great question. I'd probably still have a CT scan once a year.

Norman Swan: Just to keep yourself comfortable.

Brigid Hickey: Well, it would probably make me very anxious.

Norman Swan: And that's the other problem, is the more you do, the more
anxiety there is.

Brigid Hickey: There's a word for it, scan anxiety, scanxiety. One of the things
we wanted to look at in this was the harms of follow-up, because every day I see
patients who come and see me wound-up, anxious because they are coming to
see me and am I going to find a recurrence. And we've got to know that we are
benefiting people in order to put them through that.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much indeed.

Brigid Hickey: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Brigid Hickey is a radiation oncologist at Princess Alexandra
Hospital in Brisbane.

There are many factors that affect children's development, from the genes they
inherit from their parents, the age of their father at conception, and their
environment, especially if there is poverty. Poverty is well known to be toxic to
children. A study in the southern United States where they have the worst
poverty in the nation has looked at the brain scans of young people who have
spent years growing up in deprivation to see if a parenting program made any
difference. One of the researchers was Gene Brody from the Centre for Family
Research at the University of Georgia, Athens.

Gene Brody: Economic hardship really rips the psychological fabric of the
parents rearing children. These parents work very hard, despite living in tough
circumstances, to do their best. But the chronic day-to-day stressors associated
with poverty made them feel badly, and for some children this had the

consequence of them not doing as well as they could or reaching their potential
in school and other areas. And this jived with other research from around the
world actually, that shows that children growing up in poverty conditions where
resources are scarce but stressors are plenty tend not to develop as well
academically and socially as children who aren't battling these particular kinds of
stressors.

Norman Swan: And you have some evidence that the brains were in fact
different.

Gene Brody: You know, there were clues there where researchers would
associate living in poverty with diminished brain development, and it made us
wonder, since we follow children from preadolescents through young adulthood,
whether children who spent more years living in poverty would have smaller brain
volumes in areas of the brain that were important for their academic
development, for their memory and for their ability to cope with stress. And
unfortunately we found it was, for some children.

Norman Swan: And which parts of the brain and what sort of functionality?

Gene Brody: The parts of the brain that we focused on where the hippocampus
and the amygdala.

Norman Swan: So that's memory, emotional control, that sort of thing.

Gene Brody: Right, yes.

Norman Swan: You also looked at an intervention called Strong African
American Families which was, what, a parenting program?

Gene Brody: Yes, in 2001, 2002 we developed a program for African American
families living in the rural south that was designed to mitigate stress by
enhancing the quality of care giving that children received. And we have studied
the effectiveness of this program to promote psychological adjustment, academic
achievement, and some health outcomes as well. And that caused us to wonder
if the benefits of this program would extend to brain development. Would youth,
who at age 11 lived more years in poverty and whose brain development was
assessed at age 25, not show the deleterious effects of poverty if they had

participated and received enhanced levels of parenting that were taught by the
Strong African American Families program?

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Gene Brody: We were delighted to find it did. So the association or the link
between poverty and diminished brain development was found only for children
who did not participate in the prevention program.

Norman Swan: And what were the elements of this program, what were you
teaching parents to do? Because you probably know in Australia we have
developed one particular parenting program which is quite popular
internationally. What were you doing with these parents, what were you teaching
them?

Gene Brody: First I want to give a shout-out to Professor Matt Sanders…

Norman Swan: At Griffith University.

Gene Brody: Whose prevention programs are internationally known. Our
program was a little different than Professor Sanders' in that the rural Southern
context that our participants grew up in are unique, and the parenting practices
that are successful in the 'black belt' might be different than parenting practices in
the northern parts of the United States or in very urban areas. So we spent 10
years documenting what were the parenting processes that enhanced the
development of children in the rural south. And we settled on and focused on a
few things that really tended to matter. And these things were providing
emotional support for children, increase the amount of time that parents spend
with their children, increase the use of a parenting dynamic which involves high
levels of control laced with high levels of warmth. The kids know that the reason
their parents are keeping them in tow and being very vigilant about their children
is that they often live in some dangerous circumstances which require that
protection. Another thing we did was to enhance how routinised the home
environments were.

Norman Swan: So making them less chaotic.

Gene Brody: Making them much less chaotic, much more predictable, making
sure there was a time and place for them to do their studies, and all the while
increasing their presence at their children's school. One of the things that we find
is the more that home environments are routinised and predictable and parents
show up at school, schools treat the parents differently and in turn the children
benefit more from the teacher's attention at school. And over time this particular
formulation of parenting practices really has been shown to aid not only
psychosocial development but health, and now it appears to expand into the
brain.

Norman Swan: And just finally, Gene Brody, the applicability to other areas?

Gene Brody: This program has now been disseminated into 40 communities
across the United States, and we are optimistic about its ability to continue to
enhance the development of African American youth, and time will tell.

Norman Swan: Thanks for joining us on the Health Report.

Gene Brody: Glad to be here, thank you for asking me.

Norman Swan: Gene Brody is the director of the Centre for Family Research at
the University of Georgia, Athens.

You've been listening to the Health Report, I'm Norman Swan, I hope you'll join
me next week.
